source: Threshold values as they are commonly cited in lending and personal-finance guidance: the 28/36 housing and back-end rules used by mortgage underwriters, the 30%/10% credit-utilisation figures repeated by the bureaus, and the 3-6 month emergency-fund range. Where no convention exists the band is marked null and the ratio is reported without a verdict.
confidenceNote: Thresholds are rules of thumb and lending conventions, not measured findings. A ratio outside a band is a prompt to look, never a verdict — several of these bands are wrong for particular lives by design.
note: SPEC.md Section 13, Tier 18/19. `direction` says which way is healthier: 'lower' means a smaller number is better. `good` is the edge of the comfortable zone and `warn` the edge of the uncomfortable one; for 'higher' ratios good is the floor to clear. A null band means no convention worth quoting exists — the ratio still computes, it just gets no colour.

debtToIncome.note: The 36% back-end rule used by mortgage underwriters.

savingsRate.note: Matches the FOO benchmark floor in data/foo_rules.json.

emergencyFundMonths.note: The 3-6 month range. Both edges are conventions, not findings.

liquidityRatio.note: Same shape as emergency-fund cover, measured on all liquid assets.

runwayMonths.note: Cash over burn rate — the same arithmetic, named the way people ask for it.

netWorthToIncome.note: No single threshold: the useful benchmark is age-based, and that is the Retirement Savings Multiple.

solvencyRatio.note: Net worth as a share of assets. Below zero means debts exceed everything owned.

currentRatio.note: Below 1 means a year of required debt payments exceeds liquid assets.

creditUtilization.note: The 30% ceiling and the 10% "excellent" figure repeated by the credit bureaus. Both are conventions about how scoring models are believed to behave, not published thresholds.

carPaymentToIncome.note: The 10-15% of take-home guidance, applied here to gross — so it reads slightly kinder than the original.

investedShare.note: Investments over everything owned. Right for a renter, wrong for someone whose wealth is a paid-off house. No band.

personalCashFlowRatio.note: What is left after everything, as a share of income.

fiRatio.note: 1.0 means portfolio income at the safe withdrawal rate covers a year of spending.

loanToValue.note: 80% is where PMI usually drops off.

cashDrag.note: Cash as a share of assets. 'Too much' depends entirely on why it is there — see the SWAN Number.

liquidToIlliquid.note: No convention. Shown because people ask for it.

revolvingShare.note: Matches the revolving-share ceiling in data/foo_rules.json.

needsToWants.note: A split, not a score. 50/30/20 lives in data/budget_templates.json.

discretionaryIncomeRatio.note: Depends on the life. No band.

realEstateConcentration.note: High concentration is normal for a homeowner and says nothing on its own.

debtPayoffVelocity.note: How much of the balance a year of payments clears. No convention.

retirementMultiple.note: Benchmarked by age in data/retirement_milestones.json, not by a fixed number.

incomeConcentration.note: No convention. One paycheque reads 100%; that is a fact about the household, not a fault.

confidenceWeightedNetWorth.note: A figure, not a ratio; compared to the plain net worth beside it on The Statement.

liquidityLadder.note: No convention; right for a renter with a brokerage, wrong for a homeowner with a 401(k).

shadowRunway.note: The same 3–6 month convention as emergency fund coverage, applied to a wider pool.

worstPlausibleYearCoverage.note: 1× is covered by definition; half-covered is the watch line, a convention chosen here.

automationRatio.note: Not computed until the Skill Stacker asks which contributions are automated.

givingRate.note: The 10% tithe is a religious convention, not a financial one; no band.

netWorthInYears.note: Reads like the FI ratio in years; benchmarked by age elsewhere, not here.

humanToFinancialCapital.note: Falls through a career by construction; no fixed number is right at every age.

bracketRoom.note: A planning figure for conversions and raises, not a health measure.

bridgeGapYears.note: Zero means no bridge is needed; a longer gap is not worse if the bridge is funded.

lifestyleInflation.note: Keep at least half of every raise: a common rule of thumb. Above 100% spending rose faster than pay.

netWorthGrowthRate.note: Depends entirely on the starting figure; no convention.

withdrawalRate.note: The 4% rule as commonly cited; 5% is where most guidance starts to worry. A convention, not a finding — sequence risk is not in it.
